opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of those design choices that sounds like an implementation detail but actually matters a lot for how the search behaves.

The way I think about it, diff-based mutations are your local exploitation operator. You take a program that's already working reasonably well, and you ask the LLM to make a targeted edit: tweak a hyperparameter, swap out a loop, fix an edge case. That's very sample-efficient when you're near a good solution, and it preserves all the scaffolding that's already working. But it has a bias. Edits tend to be incremental, and you can get stuck refining one idea when a structurally different approach would be much better.

Full program rewrites are almost the opposite. You give the model the parent, maybe some context about what's been tried, and you let it regenerate the whole thing. That's more exploratory. The model can restructure the algorithm, change the representation, try a fundamentally different strategy. The cost is that you lose some reliability. Rewrites break things more often, and you might throw away subtle details that were contributing to the score.

Crossover is the interesting third piece. In classical genetic programming, crossover on syntax trees was always a bit awkward, because splicing subtrees rarely produces anything meaningful. With LLMs, you can do something much more semantic. You show the model two or more parent programs that each do something well and ask it to combine their strengths. That gives you a way to recombine building blocks that were discovered in different lineages, which pure mutation can't really do.

So my view is that you want all three, and the real question is how you balance them. Mixing operators gives you a natural exploration–exploitation knob. Early on, or when the population looks stagnant, you lean more on rewrites and crossover to inject diversity. When you're refining a strong candidate, diffs do most of the heavy lifting. And ideally you don't hand-tune that schedule. You can treat operator choice, and even which LLM to use, as a bandit problem and adapt it based on which operators are actually producing improvements.

The other point I'd make is that these operators interact with your population structure. If you have islands or some archive that maintains diversity, crossover between islands becomes really valuable, because you're combining genuinely different solutions rather than near-copies. So it's less about any single operator being best and more about building a system where the operators, the selection, and the diversity mechanisms reinforce each other.

r001.rationale: It says full rewrites let the model try fundamentally different strategies and that rewrites can inject diversity, unlike incremental diff edits.

r002.rationale: It describes asking the model to combine strengths from two or more parent programs that each do something well.

r003.rationale: It says mixing operators supports exploration and that rewrites and crossover can inject diversity, helping the search explore different solutions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that diffs are the workhorse, but they're not sufficient on their own, and the reason comes down to what kind of search landscape you're actually in.

When you ask a model to produce a diff, you're implicitly biasing toward local moves. You take the current program, you change a loop bound, you swap an activation, you tweak a hyperparameter. And that's great for hill climbing. A lot of the gains we see in something like AlphaEvolve-style or ShinkaEvolve-style systems come exactly from that kind of steady, incremental refinement, because the model has a very good prior about what small edits tend to be safe and beneficial. The diff format also keeps context short and keeps the model focused.

But diffs have a failure mode, which is that you get stuck in a basin. If the structure of the program is wrong, if you've committed to the wrong decomposition of the problem, no sequence of small edits is going to get you out efficiently. You end up spending hundreds of evaluations polishing something that was architecturally the wrong idea. And every one of those evaluations costs you compute, sometimes a lot of compute if you're training a model as part of the fitness function.

So that's where full rewrites come in. A rewrite is essentially a long-range jump. You give the model the current program, maybe its performance history, and you say, don't patch this, rethink it. The model can bring in a completely different algorithmic idea from its pretraining. It's expensive per sample and the hit rate is lower, but when it works, it moves you to a new region of the space that diffs could never have reached. I tend to think of it as the exploration knob, and you want it on at a lower rate than mutations, but you really don't want it off.

Crossover is the interesting one, because people sometimes dismiss it as a relic of classical genetic programming, where it was mostly destructive. But with an LLM as the operator, crossover becomes something closer to conceptual synthesis. You show the model two parents that are both decent but succeed for different reasons, and you ask it to combine the ideas. The model actually understands why each one works, so it's not splicing random subtrees, it's saying, this parent has a nice initialization trick and that parent has a better scheduling scheme, let's merge those. That's recombination at the level of ideas, and in practice it's one of the more sample-efficient operators we've looked at, because it reuses information that the population has already paid to discover.

The way I'd frame the whole thing is that you're really managing a portfolio. Diffs for exploitation, rewrites for exploration, crossover for recombining what you've already learned. And the fun engineering question is how to adaptively allocate between them. You can do something bandit-like, track which operator has been producing improvements recently, and shift the sampling probability accordingly. Early in a run, rewrites and crossover tend to pay off more because the population is diverse and immature. Later, once you've found a good structure, diffs dominate. If you fix those ratios by hand you'll be wrong for most of the run.

And one last thing I'd add is that the operators interact with how you maintain the population. Crossover is only useful if you actually have diversity to recombine, so you need something like islands or a novelty criterion to stop everything collapsing to one lineage. Otherwise you're crossing a program with a near-copy of itself and you've just paid for an expensive diff.

r001.rationale: It says full rewrites can introduce a different algorithmic idea and move the search to a new region that diff mutations could not reach, communicating increased diversity over diffs alone.

r002.rationale: It describes combining two parents that succeed for different reasons, such as taking one parent’s initialization trick and the other’s scheduling scheme.

r003.rationale: It assigns distinct roles to diffs, rewrites, and crossover—exploitation, exploration, and recombination—and explains that rewrites can reach regions diffs cannot, supporting discovery through operator diversity.

astra-6.text:
I think they give you different ways of moving through the search space. With a diff-based mutation, you’re taking an existing program and making a fairly targeted change. That’s useful when the structure is already good and you want to refine it. But you can also get stuck optimizing within that structure.

A rewrite gives you an opportunity to change the representation itself. You might preserve the underlying idea while expressing it in a way that makes further improvements easier. Of course, you can also lose useful details, so I wouldn’t want every mutation to be a complete rewrite.

Crossover is interesting because different candidates may have discovered complementary ideas. Can you take the useful part of one and integrate it into another? For code, that requires more than just stitching together two strings. The pieces have assumptions and dependencies, and a language model can potentially help reconcile those.

So I see these operators as complementary. Diffs give you local refinement; rewrites and crossover offer ways to make larger moves. The empirical question is whether those larger moves produce enough useful novelty to justify their evaluation cost. I’d want to measure that under a fixed budget, rather than assume that adding more operators necessarily makes the search better.

r001.rationale: The response says rewrites can change a program’s representation and enable larger moves, but does not clearly state that rewriting whole programs increases diversity relative to diff-based mutations alone.

r002.rationale: It describes candidates discovering complementary ideas and asks whether a useful part of one can be integrated into another.

r003.rationale: The response calls the operators complementary and mentions useful novelty, but does not clearly state that diversity among operators helps the search discover new solutions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they give you different ways of exploring the space. With a diff-based mutation, you’re usually preserving most of the existing program and making a fairly targeted change. That’s useful when you already have something promising and want to refine it, but it can also keep you close to the structure you started with.

A rewrite gives you the opportunity to change that structure more substantially. You might discover a different representation or a simpler way of expressing the algorithm that makes subsequent improvements easier. Of course, you can also lose something that was working well.

Crossover is interesting because you can try to combine ideas from different successful candidates. But code is quite context-dependent: taking a good component from one program and putting it into another doesn’t necessarily produce a good combination. The components have assumptions and dependencies.

So I’d think of these as complementary operators. The question is whether rewrites and crossover produce useful improvements that you wouldn’t get from spending the same evaluation budget on more local mutations. You want to measure that, and ideally let the search adapt how often it uses each operator.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts targeted diff mutations with rewrites that can change program structure substantially and discover a different representation, conveying broader search diversity.

r002.rationale: It describes crossover as combining ideas from different successful candidates, which conveys seeking a complementary improvement from parent programs.

r003.rationale: It says the operators may produce improvements unavailable from local mutations, but does not clearly state that diversity among operators helps discover new solutions.
